title: Small Models Are Enough to Imitate Human Choice Behaviour
hook: Fourteen models from 135M to 14B were fine-tuned on 10.7 million human decisions. In-distribution, 0.6B matched a 70B baseline — scale only started paying off on unfamiliar tasks.
key_points: Fourteen models, 135M to 14B parameters, across four architecture families, fine-tuned on Psych-101 (10.7M trial-level choices from 160 experiments).
In-distribution the models sit in a narrow band as if against a ceiling; 0.6B–1B suffices to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants.
Out-of-distribution the band opens into a much steeper scaling gradient — bigger models generalize better to novel task structure.
Masking stimulus content and outcome feedback destroys 75.7% of learned information and pushes models below chance.
That rules out the obvious shortcut: choice history alone does not explain the performance.
Permuting trial order changes nothing on independent-trial tasks but hurts where order depends on prior responses.
content_html: Fine-tuning an LLM on human behavioural data turns it into a general-purpose cognitive proxy — a stand-in participant for psychology experiments. Two questions have hung over that idea: how big does the model need to be, and is it modelling the task or exploiting a statistical shortcut?
extra_html:
The experiment

Nick Oh and Fernand Gobet trained fourteen models, 135M to 14B parameters, across four architecture families, on Psych-101 — 10.7 million trial-level choices drawn from 160 experiments. In-distribution, scale barely registered: the models fell inside a narrow band, as if against a ceiling, with 0.6B to 1B parameters enough to match a 70B baseline on held-out participants. Push them out-of-distribution, onto novel task structure, and that band opens into a markedly steeper scaling gradient where the larger models pull ahead.

To probe what the models were using, the authors ran two diagnostics. Progressively stripping four prompt channels — instructions, stimuli, feedback, choice history — across 27 experiments showed that masking stimulus content and feedback destroys 75.7% of the learned information and pushes performance below chance, so the models are not merely replaying choice history. Permuting trial order left performance intact on independent-trial tasks but degraded it where trial order depends on prior responses.

Why it matters

It's a rare case where "scale is not the answer" is the useful finding: small, cognitively fine-tuned models look promising as noise-ceiling estimators for psychological experiments, which makes the approach cheap enough to actually use. The authors are explicit about the limit — the models' scope stays bounded by the paradigms they saw in training, which is exactly where the out-of-distribution scaling gradient starts to bite.

related.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
related.hook: Loss doesn't drop randomly as models grow — it follows a smooth power law in size, data, and compute. That predictability is what made betting on bigger models rational.

flashcards.prompt: Where did model scale actually matter in this study?

choices.text: Out-of-distribution — generalizing to novel task structure
In-distribution, on held-out participants from the training paradigms
Nowhere; all fourteen models were statistically indistinguishable

flashcards.explanation_html: In-distribution the models clustered in a narrow band, with 0.6B–1B matching a 70B baseline. The steep scaling gradient only appeared out-of-distribution.

flashcards.prompt: How did the authors rule out models just parroting choice history?
flashcards.back_html: They progressively stripped prompt channels across 27 experiments. Masking stimulus content and outcome feedback destroyed 75.7% of learned information and drove models below chance — so history alone cannot account for performance.

flashcards.prompt: What did permuting trial order reveal?
flashcards.back_html: Models were invariant to order on tasks with independent trials, but sensitive where trial order is determined by prior responses — evidence they track task structure rather than a fixed sequence.
